demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Vignette: Layla, Age 31

Layla was twenty-eight when it happened. She had been driving home from a late dinner with friends, tired but not impaired, navigating a stretch of road she had taken hundreds of times before. A cyclist came out of nowhere — or that is how she remembers it, though she knows, in the rational part of her mind, that he had been there, that the light was ambiguous, that the investigation found no criminal negligence on her part. None of that has ever mattered much. What she carries is the sound — a dull, terrible impact — and then the sight of him crumpled on the pavement, his leg bent at an angle that still visits her in the middle of the night. He survived, but lost the use of that leg permanently. Layla has never stopped believing she took something irreplaceable from him.

In the weeks that followed, she functioned in the way people do when functioning is the only alternative to falling apart. She went through the legal process, spoke to insurance adjusters, answered questions in a flat, careful voice. Her then-husband tried to be supportive, but she found herself unable to tolerate his reassurances. Every time he told her it was an accident, she felt a surge of something close to rage — as if his kindness was a kind of erasure. The marriage had already been strained, and within a year it was over. She does not blame the accident entirely, but she does not separate it from the divorce either.

Layla works as a social media manager for a mid-sized lifestyle brand, spending most of her day behind a screen, curating images of ease and beauty. There is a particular irony she is aware of but cannot fully articulate — that her professional life requires her to project warmth and lightness while her inner life feels like something permanently shadowed. She is good at her job. She meets deadlines, attends video calls, writes copy that sounds effortless. But several times a week, a photograph will cross her desk — a cyclist, a street at night, a car advertisement — and her chest tightens in a way that takes the rest of the afternoon to ease. She has learned to close the image quickly and keep moving.

Sleep is unreliable. She falls asleep without much trouble most nights, but wakes at two or three in the morning with her heart already racing, the dream dissolving but leaving behind a residue of dread she cannot shake. She lies in the dark and replays the moment — not the whole sequence, just that sound, and then his leg. She has tried leaving the television on, keeping her phone nearby, anything to interrupt the silence that seems to invite it back.

She avoids driving after dark whenever possible. She takes rideshares to evening events and has constructed a set of justifications — parking, drinking, convenience — that she offers to friends without mentioning the real reason. Daytime driving is manageable, though she grips the wheel more tightly than she used to and finds herself scanning the edges of the road with an alertness that exhausts her. Cyclists, in particular, cause a reflexive tightening in her body that she has never been able to train away.

What troubles Layla most is not the fear but the shame. She describes herself, in quiet moments, as someone who hurt a person and walked away from it. That the law absolved her is, in her mind, beside the point. She thinks about him — the cyclist, whose name she knows but rarely allows herself to say — and wonders whether he thinks about her. Whether he hates her. Whether he should. She has written him letters that she has never sent, drafts saved in a folder on her laptop she opens occasionally and then closes without reading all the way through. She is not sure what she would want him to say back. She is not sure forgiveness is something she believes she is allowed to want.
